sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ahriman** ​(*ahriman*) ‌— Evil, ‌Destruction, ​Lies ​· Evil ​spirit, ​destructive ​mind — ‌belongs ​to ​the ‌Zoroastrian tradition, ​where ‌it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the ​domain ​"Evil, Destruction, ​Lies". ​The ‌name means ​"Evil ‌spirit, ​destructive mind".

‌**Ahriman** ​is ‌evil, ​destruction, lies. ‌The ​name ​means "Evil ‌spirit, ‌destructive ‌mind" ​and belongs ​to ‌the ​zoroastrian tradition.

​PuniCodex ‌restores ​the name ​as ‌**Ahriman** ​and ‌serves its ​temple ​at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/ahriman/). ​The ‌restoration ‌needs no ​distinctive ‌letters ​or ​diacritics its ‌ASCII ‌form ‌would lose, ‌which ​places ‌the ​name in ​Tier ​2. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form ​*ahriman* survives ‌as ​a ​modern ​convenience imposed ‌by ​the ‌early domain-name ​system; ‌the ​restoration, ‌not the ‌fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ​project ‌defends as ‌philologically ​complete.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Avestan as ​**𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 ​𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎**. Etymologically ​it ​means ‌"Evil spirit, ​destructive ​mind".

The ‌ASCII ​form ‌*ahriman* survives ​only ‌because the ​early ​domain-name ​system could ​not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Ahriman** recovers ​the ‌full ‌diacritic detail ‌of ​the scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ​in the ​address ‌bar. The ​restoration ​needs ‌no distinctive ​letters ‌or ​diacritics its ​ASCII ​form would ​lose, ‌which ‌places the ​name ‌in Tier ​2.

​The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

‌- **a** ‌→ ​**A** ‌— Same
​- ​**h** → ​**h** ‌— ​Same
- ​**r** ​→ **r** ‌— ​Same
​- **i** ​→ ‌**i** — ​Same
‌- ​**m** → ‌**m** ​— Same
‌- ‌**a** ​→ **a** ​— ​Same
- ​**n** ‌→ ‌**n** — ​Same

sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/ahriman/** — ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

‌- ​**ahriman** ‌— ​The canonical ‌restored ​form ​Ahriman.

​For the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ‌is: ​Say ‌"ahriman" ​with the ‌stress ​and ‌length ​implied by ​the ‌scholarly ‌restoration ‌"Ahriman".

​The ASCII ​form ‌"ahriman" ​is ​a DNS ‌compromise; ​the ​restoration ‌"Ahriman" preserves ​the ‌name's ​scholarly ​dignity.

The ​pronunciation ​given ‌above ‌reconstructs the ​sound ‌world ​in ​which ‌Ahriman was ‌invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should not ‌expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not ​a performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌restoration ​Ahriman ‌keeps the ​prosodic ‌information ‌visible ​even when ​the ​name ​is ‌typed in ‌plain ​ASCII.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌preserved ​in ​Avestan ​as **𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 ​𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎** ​— ‌Avestan ​alphabet ​(Iranian), ‌attested ​Avestan ‌canon, ​c. ‌1000 ​BCE ​– ​600 CE ​(written ​tradition ‌4th–6th ​c. ‌CE), ​in ‌Eastern ​Iran. ‌The ​script ‌is ​written right-to-left.[^1]

​The ‌scholarly ‌transliteration ‌is ​*aŋra ​mainiiu* ‌(Avestan ​scholarly), ​giving ‌the ​normalized ​reading ‌/aŋˈra ˈmaɪ.niː.ju/.

​The ‌rendering ​proceeds ​step ​by ​step:

‌- ‌Written ​aŋra ‌mainiiu ​in ​the ‌Avesta (Gathic ‌nom. ‌aŋrō ‌mainiiuš, ​Yasna ‌45.2; ​Younger ​form ​at ‌Vendidad ​19.1)
​- ​The Younger ‌spelling ​writes ​the ​ending ‌with ​two ‌i-letters ​(…mainiiu)
‌- ​'Ahriman' ‌is ‌the ​Middle Persian ​(Pahlavi) ​development ​of ‌the ‌same ​name

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Ahriman ‌place ​evil, destruction, ​lies ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

Ahriman ‌appears ​in ‌zoroastrian tradition ​as ​evil, destruction, ​lies. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Evil ​spirit, destructive ‌mind", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about this ​figure.

‌### ​Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ‌later tradition-keepers ​preserved ​Ahriman ‌in ritual, ​text, ​and iconography, ‌ensuring ​the ​name survived ‌into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

​The myths ​of ​Ahriman survive ‌in ‌fragments, ​summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. Each ​version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ​— ‌poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ‌PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ​privilege ‌a single ​version; ​it gathers ​the ‌attestations ​so that ‌readers ​can compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Ahriman ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Ahriman ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Zoroastrian ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming 𐬀𐬢𐬭𐬀 ‌𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬥𐬌𐬌𐬎, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult ​remains ​tied to ​evil ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To ​contemplate ‌Ahriman is ‌to ​hold ​the ​idea of ​evil, ​Destruction, ‌Lies ​in the ​mind ‌and ​to ask ‌what ​of ‌it ​endures. The ​name ​means ​"Evil ​spirit, destructive ‌mind" ​— ‌and ​a name ‌that ​carries ‌its ​meaning so ‌openly ​invites ​meditation ‌rather than ‌mere ‌recollection. ​The tradition ​remembers ‌the ​name ​as evil, ‌Destruction, ​Lies ​· ‌Evil spirit, ​destructive ‌mind.

​Sit ​with the ​restored ​form ‌— ‌Ahriman — ​and ‌the ​diacritics themselves ​become ‌the ‌practice: ‌each mark ‌is ​a ‌small ​act of ​attention, ​a ‌refusal ​to let ​the ​plain ‌ASCII ​form *ahriman* ​stand ​in ‌for ​the whole. ‌What ​the ‌tradition preserved ​in ‌this ‌name, ​the restoration ​asks ​the ​reader ‌to preserve ‌in ​turn.
